# Imports

```{r}
library(tidyverse)

pokemon_2026 = read.csv("data/dataset_2026-10-23.csv")
```

# Number of NA's for Each Column

```{r}
pokemon_2026 %>%
  summarise(across(everything(), ~ sum(is.na(.))))
```

# Estimates of Location

Estimates of Location  are a way to get an idea of the typical value for each feature variable (numerical). 

## Prices 

### Mean

```{r}
mean(pokemon_2026$low, na.rm = TRUE)
mean(pokemon_2026$mid, na.rm = TRUE)
mean(pokemon_2026$high, na.rm = TRUE)
```
### Trim Mean

```{r}
mean(pokemon_2026$low, na.rm = TRUE, trim = 0.1)
mean(pokemon_2026$mid, na.rm = TRUE, trim = 0.1)
mean(pokemon_2026$high, na.rm = TRUE, trim = 0.1)
```
### Summary

```{r}
summary(pokemon_2026$low)
summary(pokemon_2026$mid)
summary(pokemon_2026$high)
```

From this trim and our summary statistics you can tell that the data is heavily skewed. Next we will be looking into the distributions of the prices. 

## HP

```{r}
summary(pokemon_2026$hp)
```
We can infer that the health of each Pokemon is not as skewed as the price, let's look at this data in this distribution

# Visualizing Distributions

## Market Prices of Cards with Boxplots

```{r}
ggplot(pokemon_2026, aes(x = low)) +
  geom_boxplot() 
```

```{r}
ggplot(pokemon_2026, aes(x = mid)) +
  geom_boxplot() 
```

```{r}
ggplot(pokemon_2026, aes(x = high)) +
  geom_boxplot()
```

We can tell from this chart that our data is heavily skewed for the lowest market price, middle market price, and highest market price. 

## HP with Histograms

```{r}
ggplot(pokemon_2026, aes(x = hp)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40) + 
  labs(title = "Distribution of Pokemon HP", 
       x = "HP (Health Points)") 

```

# Number of Attacks with Density Plot

```{r}
ggplot(pokemon_2026, aes(x = age_years)) +
  geom_density(fill = "skyblue") +
  labs(title = "Density Curve of Number of Attacks",
       x = "Number of Years Since the Card First Released")
```

## Number of Attacks in Years with Frequency Tables 

```{r}
breaks <- seq(from=min(pokemon_2026[['n_attacks']]),
                to=max(pokemon_2026[['n_attacks']]), length=4)
pop_freq <- cut(pokemon_2026[['n_attacks']], breaks=breaks,
                right=TRUE, include.lowest=TRUE)
table(pop_freq)
```

# Exploring Variability

## Standard Deviation and Related Estimates

```{r}
sd(pokemon_2026$low, na.rm = TRUE)
sd(pokemon_2026$mid, na.rm = TRUE)
sd(pokemon_2026$high, na.rm = TRUE)
sd(pokemon_2026$hp, na.rm = TRUE)
sd(pokemon_2026$n_attacks, na.rm = TRUE)
sd(pokemon_2026$age_years, na.rm = TRUE)
```

## HP with Mean Absolute Deviation

Mean Absolute Deviation is a way to find the measure of variance for a column which has extreme outliers. 

```{r}
mean(abs(pokemon_2026$mid - mean(pokemon_2026$mid, na.rm = TRUE)), na.rm = TRUE)
```
We can see that this differs widely from the standard deviation which was given to us above for the mid column. 

## Quartiles (IQR)

```{r}
IQR(pokemon_2026$low, na.rm = TRUE)
IQR(pokemon_2026$mid, na.rm = TRUE)
IQR(pokemon_2026$high, na.rm = TRUE)
IQR(pokemon_2026$hp, na.rm = TRUE)
IQR(pokemon_2026$age_years, na.rm = TRUE)
```

We can use this to find the range of (x, y) where x is the 1nd quartille and is the 3rd quantile. 

```{r}
quantile(pokemon_2026$low, probs = c(0.25, 0.75), na.rm = TRUE)
quantile(pokemon_2026$mid, probs = c(0.25, 0.75), na.rm = TRUE)
quantile(pokemon_2026$high, probs = c(0.25, 0.75), na.rm = TRUE)
quantile(pokemon_2026$age_years, probs = c(0.25, 0.75), na.rm = TRUE)
quantile(pokemon_2026$hp, probs = c(0.25, 0.75), na.rm = TRUE)
```

# Binary and Categorical Data

A good majority of the data we have collected is either categorical or binary. Here are a couple of ways in which to explore these data types

# Mode

What is the most common category in these columns

```{r}
get_mode = function(v, na.rm = TRUE) {
  
  # Remove NAs
  v_clean <- v[!is.na(v)]
  
  if (length(v_clean) == 0) {
    return(NA)
  }
  
  uniqv <- unique(v_clean)
  uniqv[which.max(tabulate(match(v_clean, uniqv)))]
}

get_mode(pokemon_2026$series)
get_mode(pokemon_2026$poke_type)
get_mode(pokemon_2026$artist)
```

# Frequency Table

```{r}
poke_table = table(pokemon_2026$poke_type)
poke_table
```


# Correlation

correlation is defined from the book as a measure that quantifies the strength and direct of a linear relationship. We can filter our dataset to only numerical column in order to find the correlation between our nuemrica variables

```{r}
numeric_only_poke = pokemon_2026 %>%
  select(where(is.numeric))


cor(numeric_only_poke, method = "pearson", 
    use = "complete.obs")
```

From here we can get a good idea of what could be correlated and we can go through and graph a correlation in order to get an idea of it's strength and direction

```{r}
ggplot(pokemon_2026, aes(x = mid, y = low)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
  labs(title = "The Lowest Market Price by The Highest Market Price of a Card")
```
```{r}
ggplot(pokemon_2026, aes(x = log_price, y = number_int)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
  labs(title = "The Log Middle Market Price by the Number of Cards")
```
